report:
## Conclusion

The evidence strongly supports "no" — hydroxychloroquine does **not** reduce the likelihood of dying from COVID‑19, and some analyses suggest it may even be associated with slightly higher mortality.

**Key evidence:**

1. **RECOVERY trial (UK)** — the largest randomized controlled trial (RCT) of COVID-19 treatments — found "no significant difference in mortality" between hospitalized patients given hydroxychloroquine versus usual care, leading investigators to halt that treatment arm early for futility (https://www.recoverytrial.net/results/hydroxychloroquine-results).

2. **WHO Solidarity Trial**, one of the largest global RCTs, concluded that hydroxychloroquine (along with remdesivir, lopinavir, and interferon) "appeared to have little or no effect on hospitalized COVID-19, as indicated by overall mortality" (https://www.who.int/news-room/questions-and-answers/item/coronavirus-disease-covid-19-hydroxychloroquine).

3. A large international collaborative **meta-analysis published in Nature Communications** (Axfors et al.) pooling published and unpublished RCT data found that hydroxychloroquine treatment was associated with **increased** mortality in COVID-19 patients, not decreased (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-021-22446-z).

4. A systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs (Kashour et al.) similarly found no mortality benefit from hydroxychloroquine use in COVID-19 patients (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8013604/).

**Caveat:** A more recent 2025 Nature Communications commentary re-analyzing statistical methods argued the original meta-analysis's "increased mortality" signal may be overstated depending on model choice, but even that reanalysis did **not** find any mortality *benefit*—only debated whether harm was significant.

**Bottom line:** Multiple large, well-designed RCTs (RECOVERY, Solidarity) and meta-analyses consistently show hydroxychloroquine provides no reduction in COVID-19 mortality, and it may carry increased risk. Your "no" answer is well supported by the highest-quality evidence available.
